items.title: liulab-molviz
items.text:
molviz draws DNA. Hand it a plasmid or a PCR product, and it draws a map in the browser. You can turn the map, zoom in and read the bases on both strands. molviz also draws figures to set beside a protocol step, agarose gels with their expected bands, and plates with what each well holds. From Python, it writes each drawing as a page that opens offline, or as an SVG, PNG or PDF file.

molviz draws only what you hand it. Your code finds the cut sites, translates each coding sequence and places the features. molviz lays them out and draws them.

items.title: See a map
items.text:
This is pUC19-GFP, the pUC19 vector with GFP put in by Golden Gate assembly. The viewer draws it in your browser when the page opens.

Rest the pointer on a feature to see its name, type and place. Scroll over the circle to turn it. The switches above the map show it as a line, or show its bases.

items.title: Install it
items.text:
molviz is on PyPI as liulab-molviz. To add it to a pixi project, run:

pixi add python=3.13
pixi add --pypi liulab-molviz

Add Python first, because pixi needs Python to install a package from PyPI.

items.title: Go further
items.text:
• The tutorial installs molviz and draws a plasmid you type as a circle, one step at a time.
  • Choose a drawing says which drawing answers which question, and links to the guide for each one.
  • The record format lists every key a record holds. The Python API lists each function, the options that draw takes, and the command line.
  • What molviz draws and what you hand it says which work is your code's and which is molviz's.

items.title: Python API
items.text:
This page lists the molviz package's names, each as its docstring describes it. Import each one from molviz, as in molviz.draw. A page that draws in the browser calls the viewer itself, through the names on the JavaScript API page.

Each input's keys are on its format's page: record, gel, plate and figure. Export SVG, PNG and PDF uses Drawing.write, and Put drawings in your own page uses still_svg, font_rules and viewer_script.

class Drawing:
    """An input drawn, as each of molviz's draw calls returns it. A caller never makes one.

    Attributes
    ----------
    hidden : list[dict[str, Any]]
        The labels left out because they would overlap: of what a file draws at full size, or
        of what a page opens on. Each is the viewer's ``Hidden``, defined in its
        ``labels.ts``: its ``kind``, ``name``, and ``spans`` or, for a cut site, an insertion
        or a disagreement at a point, its point ``at``.
    notice : str
        The sentence that counts the hidden labels by kind, worded by the viewer, such as
        "3 cut sites and 1 primer are hidden". Empty when nothing hides.
    """

    def __init__(
        self,
        name: str,
        data: dict[str, Any] | list[dict[str, Any]],
        drawn: dict[str, Any],
        title: str,
        options: dict[str, Any] | None = None,
    ) -> None:
        # `drawn` is the viewer's drawing of `data`, the input called `name`. A page titled
        # `title` hands that input's draw call `data`, then any `options`.
        self._name = name
        # Each argument of the draw call by its block's id on a page. As text, so a change the
        # caller makes to an input afterwards never reaches the page.
        given = {name: data} if options is None else {name: data, "options": options}
        self._arguments = {block: _json(value) for block, value in given.items()}
        self._title = title
        self._svg: str = drawn["svg"]
        self._pages: list[str] = drawn["pages"]
        self.hidden: list[dict[str, Any]] = drawn["hidden"]
        self.notice: str = drawn["notice"]

    def write(self, path: str | PathLike[str], dpi: float = 300) -> None:
        """Write the drawing to ``path``, in the format its ending names, in any case.

        The endings are ``.html``, a page that opens offline; ``.svg``; ``.png``, at ``dpi``
        pixels per inch; and ``.pdf``. One unit of the drawing is one point, so a PDF page is
        the drawing's own size and a PNG is that size in print, cut to whole pixels. A PDF of a
        record with its sequence view has the map on the first page and the rows on the pages
        after. A record's page draws it with the viewer; any other page holds its still SVG and
        no viewer.

        Raises
        ------
        ValueError
            If the ending is none of those, or if a PNG at ``dpi`` would pass 2**22 pixels on a
            side or 2**28 in all.
        """
        path = Path(path)
        match path.suffix.lower():
            case ".html":
                if self._name in _LIVE:
                    page = _page(self._title, self._name, self._arguments)
                else:
                    page = _still_page(self._title, self.still_svg())
                path.write_bytes(page.encode())
            case ".svg":
                path.write_bytes(self._svg.encode())
            case ".png":
                most = _most_dpi(self._svg)
                if dpi > most:
                    raise ValueError(
                        f"cannot write {path!s}: a PNG of this drawing is drawn at up to "
                        f"{math.floor(most):,} dpi, not {dpi:g}; write a PDF, which draws at any size"
                    )
                import vl_convert

                # vl-convert ships no type stub, so pyright cannot see its functions.
                png = vl_convert.svg_to_png(self._svg, ppi=dpi)  # pyright: ignore[reportAttributeAccessIssue]
                path.write_bytes(png)
            case ".pdf":
                path.write_bytes(_pdf(self._pages))
            case _:
                raise ValueError(
                    f"cannot write {path!s}: its ending must be .html, .svg, .png or .pdf"
                )

    def still_svg(self) -> str:
        """Return the drawing as SVG with real text, for a page that holds no viewer.

        It is laid out as the ``.svg`` file is and hides the same labels. Each text is held to
        its measured width, and each hover is a ``<title>``. It draws in the viewer's faces
        only on a page that writes ``font_rules()`` once, in a ``<style>`` element.
        """
        arguments = f"[{','.join(self._arguments.values())}]"
        return call_json(self._name, "still", arguments)["svg"]

def draw_figure(records: list[dict[str, Any]], **options: Any) -> Drawing:
    """Draw ``records`` stacked top to bottom, each with ``options``, checking all with the viewer.

    The options are `draw`'s, shared by every record. A name to highlight must name something
    in at least one record. A page written from it is titled with the records' names, joined by
    commas.

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        If a record breaks the format, or else if an option is unknown or wrong for any record.
        The message names every problem by its path, a record's under ``records``.
    TypeError
        If a value has no JSON form, such as a set.

    Examples
    --------
    >>> p = {"name": "p", "circular": False, "bases": "ACGT"}
    >>> draw_figure([p, {**p, "name": "q"}], highlight=["lacZ"])
    Traceback (most recent call last):
    ...

items.title: Options
items.text:
draw takes these options by name, and so does draw_figure, for every record it stacks. Each says what the drawing starts with. An option it does not know is an error, and one left out takes its default. span counts bases as the record format's coordinates do. Choose what a map shows and Show the bases use each option in turn.

Option What it does Default span Draws only the bases from start to end, as in {"start": 10, "end": 500}. start counts from 0, and the base at end is not drawn. The line is numbered as the record is. On a circular record, end may pass the record's length to run across the origin. the whole record map The map to draw: "circle" or "line". The circle draws a circular record whole, so a linear record, or a span short of the whole record, must be drawn as "line". "circle" for a circular record drawn whole, else "line" types_off The feature types to leave out. A type the record does not have is ignored. ["source"] kinds_off The kinds of thing to leave out: any of "features", "primers", "cuts", "insertions", "reads", "disagreements" and "tracks". [] enzymes The enzymes whose cut sites are drawn. A name matches in any case. A name that does not cut the record is ignored. each enzyme that cuts the record once highlight The names to light up: a feature, a primer, an insertion, a read, a disagreement, a track, or an enzyme, which lights every site it cuts. All else turns one pale grey, and nothing moves. Where labels crowd, a lit label is the last to hide. A name in any case matches. A name that matches nothing in the record is an error. [] sequence_view Draws the sequence view: the bases in rows, on both strands, with each thing drawn on them at its bases. On a page it sits beside the map, or under it when the room is narrow. In a file it sits under the map, and a PDF has the map on its first page and the rows on the pages after. It draws at most SEQUENCE_VIEW_LIMIT bases, 100,000, so past that true is an error. false bases_per_row How many bases a row of the sequence view holds. The last row may hold fewer. Left out, a page fits its rows to the width it has, from 20 to 100 bases in steps of 10. A row too wide for the page keeps its length, and the sequence view is drawn smaller to fit. fits the width on a page, 60 in a file bottom_strand Whether the sequence view draws the bottom strand under the top one. true

items.title: Coordinates
items.text: A record counts its bases from 0, and a span {start, end} holds the bases from start up to end, but not the base at end. A reader never sees these numbers. Every label and every hover counts from 1 and includes both ends, as SnapGene and GenBank do. molviz writes them that way. This page explains why the record counts one way and the drawing another, and how a span crosses the origin of a circular record. The record format states each rule in full.

items.title: A span counts from 0 and stops before its end
items.text:
In pUC19-GFP, GFP is the span {"start": 395, "end": 1112}. Counted from 0, it holds the bases at 395 to 1111. A reader sees it as 396 .. 1112.

Counting this way keeps the arithmetic plain:

  • A span's length is end - start, here 717 bases, with no 1 to add.
  • Two spans that touch share a number. The lac promoter in pUC19-GFP is three segments, from 1173 to 1180, 1180 to 1198 and 1198 to 1204. Each starts where the one before it ends.
  • It is how Python slices text, so bases[395:1112] gives GFP's bases. Biopython, BED files and the lab's cloning tools count the same way, so your code can hand its numbers over as they are.

Counting from 1 with both ends included is how people read a map. A person says "base 396", not "the base at index 395". So the record keeps the form that code gets right, and molviz turns it into the form people read when it writes a label.

items.title: A point between bases is the count of bases before it
items.text:
A cut, an insertion, and a disagreement where a read adds bases all lie between two bases, not on one. Such a point is the number of bases before it. That number is also the position, from 1, of the base it follows. So a cut after base 406 is 406, and its label reads (406) with no change. On a circular record the origin is 0, never the record's length.

A single base, such as a base a primer does not pair with, is its index from 0. It is always below the record's length, even inside a span across the origin.

items.title: A span across the origin ends past the length
items.text:
A circular record has no real start. Its origin is only where the numbering begins, and a site or a feature can lie over it. Such a span lets end pass the record's length. pUC19-GFP is 3,347 bp, and its BsmBI site is {"start": 3343, "end": 3349}: the last four bases and the first two. A reader sees it as 3344 .. 2.

There were two other ways to write it, and both cost more:

  • An end lower than its start, as SnapGene prints it. Then every length, and every test of whether a span holds a base, needs a second case for a span across the origin.
  • Two spans, split at the origin. Then the site is no longer one span. Nothing in the data would tell it apart from a feature that really is made of two pieces.

With end past the length, end - start is still the span's length, here 6. A span runs at most once around the record.

The span option follows the same rule. With {"start": 3300, "end": 3400}, the drawing below is the 100 bases across pUC19-GFP's origin, drawn as a line. The ruler goes from 3340 on to 10, the thick tick marks the origin, and the title gives the stretch as 3301 .. 53. One BsmBI cut lies just past the origin, at 3.

items.title: A joined feature's segments run in order
items.text:
A feature can be made of several segments. In pUC19-GFP, lacZα has two, from 145 to 395 and from 1112 to 1130, because GFP was put in between them. A feature lists its segments in order of their starts. On a circular record, a segment after the origin is counted past the length, as a span across the origin is.

On a linear record, a feature may run off the end and on again from the start, but only once. That happens on a PCR product that starts inside a gene, as when a plasmid's backbone is amplified from a primer inside lacZα. The one segment that starts lower than the segment before it marks where the feature runs off the end. Splitting such a feature in two would show the reader two features where SnapGene shows one, and break its translation.

items.title: Pages, files and still drawings
items.text: molviz writes a drawing in three forms: a page that a browser draws, a file, and a still drawing for a page of your own. All three draw the same picture, laid out by the same code. They differ in what a reader can do with the drawing and in where it can go.

items.title: A page is for a reader with a browser
items.text:
A drawing's write("map.html") writes a page: one HTML file that opens offline in any browser. It loads nothing over the network. The fonts are inside it, and so is everything it draws. You can send it by email or attach it to a lab notebook entry, and it opens with nothing else installed.

A record's page also carries the viewer, the script that lays the record out and draws it when the page opens. The reader can then flip a circular record between the circle and the line, switch kinds, feature types and enzymes on and off, zoom, turn the circle, show the bases, and select and copy them. Every item stays in the page behind its switch, even one the options turned off, so the reader can bring it back. Each base and each label is real text, so the browser's find works on it.

A gel, a plate or a figure has nothing to switch, so its page holds a still drawing and no viewer. That keeps the page small.

items.title: A file is for slides, papers and print
items.text:
An .svg, .png or .pdf file holds the drawing itself. Python writes it with no browser. It runs the viewer's own code inside Python, then turns the SVG into a PNG or a PDF. A file and a page are laid out by the same code, so a script with no screen draws the map you see in a browser.

A file differs from a page in three ways:

  • It draws only what is on. An item the options leave out, such as the primers when kinds_off names them, is not in the file at all.
  • Each letter is an outline, not text. The file looks the same in every program and needs no font, but you can't search or copy its text.
  • Nothing in it can be switched or zoomed. Its hidden labels stay hidden, and the drawing's hidden lists them.

Each format has its use:

  • SVG to edit in a drawing program such as Inkscape or Illustrator, or to show as a picture in a web page.
  • PDF for papers and reports, since it stays sharp at any size. Its page is the drawing's own size, with no margin, so it drops into a figure with nothing to crop. To print it on paper, use the "fit to page" setting of your PDF reader. A record drawn with its sequence view has the map on the first page and the rows of bases on the pages after it.
  • PNG for slides and for anything that takes only pictures, at the dpi you ask for. molviz refuses a PNG of a very large drawing at a high dpi, and its message points you to the PDF, which has no such limit.

items.title: A still drawing is for a page of your own
items.text:
A still drawing is SVG with real text and no viewer, written into a page. It is laid out once, so a reader can't zoom it or switch it, but can find and copy its text. It draws in molviz's fonts once the page holds the font rules, which molviz.font_rules() returns. One copy of the font rules serves every still drawing on the page.

still_svg() returns a drawing in this form. It suits a page that holds many drawings, such as a protocol with a figure beside each step. Each drawing adds only its own SVG to the page, and the page carries no viewer. To draw a record live in your own page instead, put the viewer's script, which molviz.viewer_script() returns, into the page and call the viewer's draw function. The JavaScript API lists the viewer's calls, its still ones included.

The first map below is live: try its switches. The second is the same record as a still drawing.

items.title: The same input writes the same bytes
items.text: The same input and options write the same bytes, every time, on macOS and on Linux. A drawing you keep in a repository then changes only when its input or molviz changes. A test can compare a new drawing with the one written before.

items.title: Choose by who reads it
items.text:
Who reads it What to write Someone who wants to explore the record a page, .html An audience in a talk .png, or .pdf if your slides take it A reader of a paper or a report .pdf, or .svg to edit first A visitor to your own page a still drawing, or the viewer for a live record

Export SVG, PNG and PDF and Put drawings in your own page give the steps for each.

items.title: How a drawing stays readable
items.text: A map can hold more than fits on it: a dozen features, as many primers, and a cut site for every enzyme that cuts. molviz never lets two labels overlap. A map never leaves a label out without saying so, and the sequence view leaves none out. A gel is the one exception, because it may leave out a ladder size's label without counting it. This page gives the rules a drawing keeps, so that you know what to trust in it and how to tell what it left out.

items.title: No label overlaps another
items.text: No label covers another label or the drawing, in the circle, the line or the sequence view. Where two labels would overlap, molviz hides one. It does not shrink the text, and it does not let labels pile up. Shrunk text is hard to read, and in a pile a label can sit closest to the wrong item. Either way, the reader can't tell that anything is wrong. A hidden label is counted instead, so the reader knows.

items.title: Every hidden label is counted
items.text:
A drawing that hides labels says so at the bottom right of the map, counted by kind, such as "3 cut sites and 1 primer are hidden". On a page, rest the pointer on that notice to list the hidden labels. In Python, the drawing that molviz.draw returns holds the same sentence in notice and the hidden labels in hidden, so your code can report what a file left out. No notice means every label shows.

Labels hide in a fixed order, the least useful first:

  1. The label of a dimmed item hides before the label of a lit one.
  2. Cut sites hide first, then primers, reads, features and insertions. Disagreements hide last.
  3. Among cut sites, the enzyme that cuts most often hides first.
  4. Where all else is equal, the longest label hides first.

The order follows what a reader looks for. A record can carry dozens of cut sites, and an enzyme that cuts many times says the least about any one place. A unique cutter, the one a cloning plan looks for, hides last among cut sites. A disagreement between a read and the record is the point of checking a clone, so it hides last of all.

A name written on its feature's own arrow never hides, since it takes no room beside the map. The sequence view hides no label at all.

On a page, a hidden label can come back. Zoom in, and the map is laid out larger. Switch off a kind you don't need, and its room goes to the rest. The notice counts again each time. A file is laid out once, at its own size, so what it hides stays hidden, and hidden lists it.

items.title: A gel leaves out a crowded size
items.text: A gel writes each ladder size beside the gel, at the height where its band runs. Two sizes can run closer than a line of text. Then the gel leaves out the smaller size's label, and it does not count it, so the drawing's hidden stays empty. The gel still draws the band, and on a page, resting the pointer on the band shows its size. A sample lane's bands and the legend's lines never hide.

items.title: A highlight moves nothing
items.text:
The highlight option names what a reader should look at. Everything else dims to one pale grey, and nothing moves. Each item stays where it would be with no highlight, so a lit drawing and a plain one line up item for item. A lit label is the last to hide.

Below, pUC19-GFP is drawn twice as a line: first plain, then with GFP and its two primers lit. Every arrow and label stays in place.

items.title: Colours follow the feature type
items.text:
A feature takes its colour from its type. Coding sequences are blue, promoters and other regulatory parts orange, terminators pink and origins yellow. Other groups of types have colours of their own, and a type in no group is light grey. The record format lists the types in each group. The colours come from Paul Tol's light scheme. Tol made it so that readers with colour blindness can tell its colours apart, and so that black text reads on each of them.

Primers are purple and insertions are red. A colour you give a feature, or one of its segments, is used instead of the colour of its type. A Sanger trace draws its four curves in the colours that trace viewers use: A green, C blue, G black and T red.

items.title: A drawing keeps a white ground
items.text: A drawing is always drawn on white, even on a page with a dark theme. Every colour above was chosen against white, so the drawing reads the same on any page and prints the same.

items.title: Positions read as the record numbers them
items.text: Every label and every hover counts from 1 and includes both ends, as SnapGene and GenBank do. A line drawn from part of a record keeps the record's numbers, and a stretch across the origin of a circular record runs from the last base on to 1. Coordinates explains how a record writes these positions.

items.title: Text you can find, files that look the same anywhere
items.text: On a page, every base and every label is real text, so the browser's find, select and copy work on it. In an SVG, PNG or PDF file, each letter is drawn as an outline instead. The file then looks the same in every program and needs no font. Pages, files and still drawings says which to choose.

items.title: What molviz draws and what you hand it
items.text: molviz draws DNA, but it knows no biology. It holds no list of enzymes, no genetic code and no aligner. Your code finds where each enzyme cuts, translates each coding sequence, finds where each primer binds and lines up each read. molviz takes those answers and draws them. It lays each item out, labels it, colours it and numbers it.
path: What molviz draws and what you hand it

items.title: Your code holds the biology
items.text:
A record holds the bases and every item drawn on them, each one already worked out:

  • A feature gives its type, strand and segments. A coding sequence also gives its translation.
  • A primer gives its bases and each site where it binds, with any base there that it does not pair with.
  • A cut gives its enzyme, the bases that enzyme recognises, and where it cuts each strand.
  • Reads, the places where a read disagrees with the record, and a Sanger trace's curves come from your sequencing analysis.

molviz draws each item where the record puts it. It does not look for more. The record format lists every key a record can hold.
path: What molviz draws and what you hand it

items.title: See it on a stretch of pUC19-GFP
items.text: The drawing below shows bases 141 to 420 of pUC19-GFP, the pUC19 vector with GFP put in by Golden Gate assembly. The stretch holds part of lacZα, which runs on the bottom strand, and the start of GFP, where GFP joins the vector. The drawing asks for two enzymes in the enzymes option, NdeI and PvuII. The record lists a cut for NdeI, so its site is marked. PvuII's site, CAGCTG, is in the bases too, at bases 306 to 311. The record lists no PvuII cut, so nothing marks it. The amino acids over lacZα and GFP are the translations the record gives.
path: What molviz draws and what you hand it

items.title: Why the viewer leaves the biology to you
items.text:
Your tools already have these answers, and your plan depends on them. The enzymes in your digest, the primers on your order sheet and the reads in your analysis are the ones your code chose. If molviz found cut sites again, it would need its own list of enzymes. Then a map could show a site your plan never uses, or miss one it does. When molviz draws only your answers, the map and the plan agree.

The code that calls molviz also has its own rules, such as which enzymes the lab stocks or how a read is trimmed. With the biology in your code, those rules stay yours, and molviz stays one small drawing tool that any code can call.

What is hard to share is the drawing itself: where each label goes, which labels hide when there is no room, and how a page lets a reader zoom, switch and select. That part molviz does once, for all the code that calls it.
path: What molviz draws and what you hand it

items.title: What molviz decides for you
items.text:
molviz still makes some choices, all of them about the drawing:

  • It checks the record before it draws. Every position must lie on the record, every span must start before it ends, and a translation must fit the bases its feature holds. An unknown key is an error, so a misspelt key fails with a message instead of being dropped.
  • It counts how often each enzyme cuts, among the cuts you list. An enzyme that cuts once, a unique cutter, is set in bold. By default the drawing shows only the unique cutters. The enzymes option names others.
  • It colours each feature by its type, unless you give a colour.
  • It draws a primer's 5' tail from the primer's bases that lie past its site.
  • It writes every position the way a reader counts, from 1. Coordinates explains why the record counts another way.
  • It places every label, and hides and counts the ones that would overlap. How a drawing stays readable gives the rules.

The check is about shape, not biology. A translation that fits its bases is drawn as you give it, even if the codons say otherwise.
path: What molviz draws and what you hand it

items.title: Gels and plates work the same way
items.text: A gel takes the size of each band in each lane. molviz does not digest a record or run a PCR to find them. Your code works out the sizes, and molviz draws where each size runs on the gel. A plate takes what each well holds, as text. A stamp, which moves wells from one plate into another, is two plates you build: the one it takes from and the one it fills. The gel format and the plate format list what each holds.
path: What molviz draws and what you hand it

items.title: One check, in Python and in the browser
items.text:
The format is defined once, in the viewer's JavaScript. Python's molviz.check and molviz.draw run that same check, so a record fails the same way in Python and on a page, with the same message. The message names each problem by its place in the record, such as features[0].segments[0].end.

Options pass through Python in the same way. The options are the viewer's, and Python adds none of its own.
path: What molviz draws and what you hand it

items.title: Choose a drawing
items.text:
molviz makes seven drawings. Three are views of one record: the circle, the line and the sequence view. The other four are a figure, a close-up, a gel and a plate. Each one answers its own question, so start from the question your reader asks.

Your reader asks Draw The call What does the plasmid hold, and where? the circle molviz.draw(record) What lies along this stretch? the line molviz.draw(record, span=...) Which bases, exactly? the sequence view molviz.draw(record, span=..., sequence_view=True) What does this step of the protocol make? a figure molviz.draw_figure(records) Does the clone match at this base? a close-up molviz.draw(checked, span=..., sequence_view=True) Which bands should the gel show? a gel molviz.draw_gel(gel) What does each well hold? a plate molviz.draw_plate(plate)

Each call takes its input as a Python dict, like the record you type in the tutorial, and draw_figure takes a list of records. Each call returns a drawing, which write saves as a page or a file. In your own web page, the molviz object that the viewer script gives the page makes the same drawings with draw, drawFigure, drawGel and drawPlate, which the JavaScript API lists. Pages, files and still drawings says which drawings a reader can zoom and switch, and which output suits which use.

The examples below draw pUC19-GFP, the pUC19 vector with GFP put in by Golden Gate assembly. The plate comes from AP-1, a project that builds a library of clones on 96-well and 384-well plates. The viewer draws each example in your browser when the page opens.

items.title: The circle: what a plasmid holds
items.text:
The circle draws a circular record whole, as a ring, so a reader sees the whole plasmid at once. Each feature is an arrow along its strand. Primers sit where they bind, and the enzymes that cut the plasmid once mark their cut sites. A circular record drawn whole opens on the circle, so the call needs no options.

drawing = molviz.draw(record)

Choose what a map shows leaves out kinds, feature types and enzymes, and lights the names that matter.

items.title: The line: what lies along a stretch
items.text:
The line draws a record, or a span of it, along a straight line, numbered as the record numbers it. It suits a linear molecule, such as a PCR product, and a part of a plasmid, such as an insert with the primers around it. Here is the GFP insert and what flanks it, bases 341 to 1210.

drawing = molviz.draw(record, span={"start": 340, "end": 1210})

A span counts bases from 0 and leaves out the base at end, so this span holds bases 341 to 1210 as the line numbers them. Any span shorter than the whole record draws as a line. To draw a whole circular record as a line, pass map="line". Draw a stretch of the record gives the steps, a span across the origin included.

items.title: The sequence view: which bases
items.text:
The sequence view draws the bases of both strands in rows. Features are bars under the bases, with the amino acids of each CDS over them. Primers sit above and below the strands, and cut sites cross them. Use it to show where a primer anneals, where an enzyme cuts or how a junction reads. Draw it over a short span, because a whole plasmid makes many rows. Here is the start of GFP, where the ATGA junction joins it to the vector.

drawing = molviz.draw(record, span={"start": 380, "end": 440}, sequence_view=True)

On a page, the sequence view sits beside the map or under it. In a PDF, its rows follow the map on pages of their own. Show the bases sets the span, the row length and the strands.

items.title: A figure: what a step makes
items.text:
A figure is a still drawing of one record, or of several stacked top to bottom. It goes beside a step of a protocol. A figure draws every record with the same options, so stacked records line up, such as a vector before and after a part goes in. This figure shows the Golden Gate product. It asks for BbsI, the enzyme of the Golden Gate step. BbsI no longer cuts the product, so the figure marks no BbsI site. It also lights both junctions.

drawing = molviz.draw_figure(
    [record], enzymes=["BbsI"], highlight=["ATGA junction", "TGGC junction"]
)

Stack records into a figure stacks the two PCR products over the plasmid they make.

items.title: A close-up: whether the clone is right
items.text:
A close-up is a still drawing of a few dozen bases around one disagreement, a place where a read differs from the record it should match. It draws the line and the sequence view over that span, with the reads on it. Here, one consensus read covers all of pUC19-GFP. At base 696, inside GFP, the record holds A and the read holds G.

A close-up has no call of its own. It is the checked record drawn over a short span, with the sequence view in one row.

drawing = molviz.draw(
    checked,
    span={"start": 665, "end": 726},
    sequence_view=True,
    bases_per_row=61,
    kinds_off=["cuts"],
    highlight=["696 A>G", "consensus.fasta"],
)
drawing.write("696.svg")

Here checked is the record with its reads and disagreements. A close-up goes into an SVG, PNG or PDF file, or into a page as the SVG text from drawing.still_svg(). In your own page, the stillSvg call of the molviz object returns the same SVG. Check a clone against its reads adds the reads and draws a close-up of each disagreement.

items.title: A gel: which bands to expect
items.text:
A gel is a simulated agarose gel, with a ladder, sample lanes and each band at its size. It holds no record, because your code works out the sizes. Here is the colony PCR that checks pUC19-GFP, with a correct clone beside the empty vector.

drawing = molviz.draw_gel(gel)

draw_gel takes no options. Draw a gel writes this gel down and draws it.

items.title: A plate: what each well holds
items.text:
A plate is a grid of wells, each with what it holds, given as text. Up to ten different contents each get a colour and a line of the legend. Past ten, every filled well takes one colour, and the legend counts the contents. Rest the pointer on a well to see what it holds. Here is AP-1's first plate of picked colonies, which has 384 wells. Each colour marks one quarter of the plate, and each quarter goes into a 96-well plate of its own.

drawing = molviz.draw_plate(plate)

draw_plate takes no options. molviz draws a stamp, which moves a pattern of wells from one plate into another, as two plates: the one it takes from and the one it fills. Draw a plate and a stamp builds this plate and a stamp from it.

items.title: Draw your first plasmid map
items.text:
In this tutorial, we type a small plasmid into Python and draw it as a map. We open the map in a browser, then write the same map as an SVG file and a PDF file.

You need pixi and a terminal. Installing molviz is the one step that needs the internet. After it, everything here runs offline.

items.title: Make a project
items.text:
First, make a pixi project for your maps, and add Python and molviz to it:

pixi init my-maps
cd my-maps
pixi add python=3.13
pixi add --pypi liulab-molviz

Add Python before molviz, because pixi needs Python to install a package from PyPI. The last command ends with a line like this one:

✔ Added liulab-molviz >=2026.10.0, <2027

Now check that molviz runs:

pixi run molviz version

It prints the version you installed, such as 2026.10.0.

items.title: Type a record
items.text:
molviz draws a record: one DNA molecule, written as a Python dict. Make a file named first_map.py in the my-maps folder, and type this into it:

import molviz

record = {
    "name": "pDemo",
    "circular": True,
    "bases": "ACGT" * 750,
    "features": [
        {"name": "Plac", "type": "promoter", "strand": 1, "segments": [{"start": 40, "end": 95}]},
        {"name": "GFP", "type": "CDS", "strand": 1, "segments": [{"start": 100, "end": 820}]},
        {"name": "AmpR", "type": "CDS", "strand": -1, "segments": [{"start": 1760, "end": 2621}]},
    ],
}
molviz.check(record)
print(record["name"], "has", len(record["bases"]), "bases")

The record has a name, says whether the molecule is circular, and holds its bases. Here the bases are a stand-in. "ACGT" * 750 repeats ACGT to make 3,000 bases. Each feature has a name, a type and a strand, and covers one or more segments of the bases:

  • The type is a feature type such as CDS or promoter. The map colours each feature by its type.
  • The strand is 1 for a feature that reads along the top strand, and -1 for one that reads along the bottom strand.
  • A segment's start and end count bases from 0, and the base at end is not part of it. GFP's segment holds 720 bases, which the map numbers 101 to 820. The record format's coordinates give the full rules.

The record format lists every key a record can hold.

Run the file:

pixi run python first_map.py

It prints pDemo has 3000 bases. molviz.check found nothing wrong with the record. When it does find a mistake, it raises an error that names the key. A strand of 3 on GFP gives features[1].strand: must be 1, -1, 0 or 2.

items.title: Draw it as a page
items.text:
Add these two lines to the end of first_map.py:

drawing = molviz.draw(record)
drawing.write("pDemo.html")

Run the file again:

pixi run python first_map.py

A new file, pDemo.html, sits beside first_map.py. Open it in your browser. You can double-click it, or run open pDemo.html on a Mac or xdg-open pDemo.html on Linux.

You see a ring with "pDemo" and "3000 bp" in its middle, and a scale of base pairs just inside it. Near the top, a short orange arrow for Plac leads into GFP, a long blue arrow that runs clockwise. AmpR, also blue, runs the other way on the far side of the ring. GFP and AmpR have their names written along them. Plac's arrow is too short for its name, so the name sits outside the ring, on a line to the arrow.

The map shows no cut sites, because the record lists none. molviz draws only what you hand it. Your own code finds the cut sites, the primers and the rest, and puts them in the record.

Now try the page:

  1. Rest the pointer on GFP. A box shows its name, its type, its place, 101 .. 820, and its length, 720 bp.
  2. Scroll over the ring to turn it.
  3. Click Line in the bar above the map. The viewer draws the plasmid along a straight line. Click Circle to bring the ring back.
  4. Click Sequence to show the bases on both strands, with each feature under them. They sit beside the map, or under it in a narrow window.

The page carries the viewer that draws it, so it opens with no server and no network.

items.title: Write an SVG and a PDF
items.text:
Add two more lines to the end of first_map.py:

drawing.write("pDemo.svg")
drawing.write("pDemo.pdf")

Run the file once more:

pixi run python first_map.py

Two new files sit beside the page: pDemo.svg and pDemo.pdf. Open each one. Both hold the same ring as the page, with no bar above it. These files don't turn or zoom. The PDF has one page, the size of the drawing.

write picks the format from the file's ending, so drawing.write("pDemo.png") writes a PNG.

items.title: Next steps
items.text:
You typed a record, drew it as a page and wrote it as two files. From here:

  • Choose a drawing shows the other drawings molviz makes, and the question each one answers.
  • The record format lists the primers, cut sites, reads and other items a record can hold.
  • The Python API lists every function, and the options that draw takes.

items.title: Check a clone against its reads
items.text:
When you sequence a clone, you compare its reads with the record you expect. molviz draws the result: where each read lies, each place where a read disagrees with the record, and a close-up of the bases around each one, with the read's trace when you have it. Your code aligns the reads and finds the disagreements. molviz draws only what you hand it.

The examples check pUC19-GFP, the pUC19 vector with GFP put in by Golden Gate assembly, against one consensus read. Save its record, puc19-gfp-product.json, beside your script. Each step shows its code, then the drawing it makes, drawn here from the same record and options.
path: Check a clone against its reads

items.title: Add the reads and the disagreements
items.text:
A read names the span of the record that it covers, and the strand it was read from. A disagreement names a place where reads differ from the record, the bases they hold there, and the reads that show it. This code adds one read that covers the whole plasmid, and its two disagreements:

import json
from pathlib import Path

import molviz

record = json.loads(Path("puc19-gfp-product.json").read_text())
record["reads"] = [{"name": "consensus.fasta", "start": 0, "end": 3347, "strand": 1}]
record["disagreements"] = [
    {
        "name": "696 A>G",
        "start": 695,
        "end": 696,
        "bases": "G",
        "reads": ["consensus.fasta"],
        "color": "#cc3311",
    },
    {
        "name": "2687 C>T",
        "start": 2686,
        "end": 2687,
        "bases": "T",
        "reads": ["consensus.fasta"],
        "color": "#bbbbbb",
    },
]
molviz.check(record)

Give a disagreement its place in one of two ways:

  • A substitution or a deletion covers bases of the record, so give it a start and an end. For a deletion, set bases to "".
  • An insertion lies between two bases, so give it at, the count of bases before it, and the bases the reads add.

The name and the colour are yours. molviz writes the name as you give it, so 696 A>G counts from 1, as a reader does. Here the code checks some regions of the plasmid, such as GFP, and a region fails when a read disagrees inside it. Red marks a change in a region that fails, and grey marks one outside every region checked. A disagreement with no colour is grey.

molviz.check raises ValueError if the record breaks the format, such as a disagreement that names a read the record doesn't hold. The record format lists every key of a read and a disagreement.
path: Check a clone against its reads

items.title: Draw the map
items.text:
Draw the record with its cut sites left out, and light the read and both disagreements:

lit = ["696 A>G", "2687 C>T", "consensus.fasta"]
molviz.draw(record, kinds_off=["cuts"], highlight=lit).write("verification.html")

The read is the ring just outside the double line that stands for the plasmid's two strands. Each disagreement is a bar among the features, in its own colour.
path: Check a clone against its reads

items.title: Draw a close-up of each disagreement
items.text:
A close-up is the record drawn over a few dozen bases around one disagreement: the line, and the sequence view in one row. To make one, draw a span of 30 bases on either side, with a row long enough to hold the whole span:

for disagreement in record["disagreements"]:
    start = disagreement["start"]
    close_up = molviz.draw(
        record,
        span={"start": start - 30, "end": start + 31},
        sequence_view=True,
        bases_per_row=61,
        kinds_off=["cuts"],
        highlight=[disagreement["name"], *disagreement["reads"]],
    )
    close_up.write(f"close-up-{start + 1}.svg")

These are the two close-ups, drawn as still drawings:

The read marks the base where it disagrees in red, whatever the colour of the disagreement's bar. To put a close-up in a page of your own, use close_up.still_svg(), which returns the same drawing as SVG text. Put drawings in your own page shows how.
path: Check a clone against its reads

items.title: Add a trace
items.text:
A Sanger read's trace is a track. Your code reads it from the sequencer's .ab1 file and adds it to the record's tracks. A track holds a curve for each of A, C, G and T, all measured at the same points, called samples. Its peaks tie a sample to the base it was read as. The record format's tracks give each key.

pUC19-GFP's consensus read has no trace, so this step draws trace-3730.json. It holds 120 bases from one Sanger read, with one base changed so that the read disagrees at 61 G>C:

trace = json.loads(Path("trace-3730.json").read_text())
molviz.draw(
    trace,
    span={"start": 30, "end": 91},
    sequence_view=True,
    bases_per_row=61,
    kinds_off=["cuts"],
    highlight=["61 G>C", "3730"],
).write("close-up-61.svg")

The trace is under the bases: four curves, after the read's name and a key to their colours. Each peak sits over the base it was read as. Over base 61, the tallest curve is C, where the record holds G.

If the read is on the bottom strand, swap each curve for the base it pairs with, A with T and C with G, so that the curves read as the top strand does. The bases in peaks then fall as the samples rise. trace-3730-reversed.json is the same read turned to the other strand:

reversed_trace = json.loads(Path("trace-3730-reversed.json").read_text())
molviz.draw(
    reversed_trace,
    span={"start": 29, "end": 90},
    sequence_view=True,
    bases_per_row=61,
    kinds_off=["cuts"],
    highlight=["60 C>G", "3730"],
).write("close-up-60.svg")

The read now sits under the bases. Over base 60, the tallest curve is G, where the record holds C.
path: Check a clone against its reads

items.title: Draw a gel
items.text:
A gel drawing shows the bands you expect beside a ladder, each band where its size runs. Set it beside a PCR or a digest in a protocol, so that the reader can compare the real gel with it.

This guide draws the colony PCR from the build of pUC19-GFP, the pUC19 vector with GFP put in by Golden Gate assembly. It checks two colonies: a correct clone, which gives two bands, and an empty vector, which gives one.

items.title: Write down the gel
items.text:
Write the gel as a Python dict. Give the ladder's name and its band sizes in base pairs. Then list the lanes in the order they run, each with its name and the sizes of its bands.

colony_pcr = {
    "title": "Colony PCR",
    "ladder": {
        "name": "NEB 100 bp DNA Ladder (N3231)",
        "bands": [100, 200, 300, 400, 500, 600, 700, 800, 900, 1000, 1200, 1517],
    },
    "lanes": [
        {"name": "Correct clone", "bands": [160, 838]},
        {"name": "Empty vector", "bands": [177]},
    ],
}

The title is optional. The gel format lists every key.

items.title: Draw it and write a file
items.text:
Call draw_gel, then write the drawing to a file. The file's ending picks its format.

import molviz

drawing = molviz.draw_gel(colony_pcr)
drawing.write("colony-pcr.svg")

The file holds this gel:

The ladder runs in the lane marked L, and the sample lanes follow it, numbered in order. The legend under the gel names each lane and its sizes. Rest the pointer on a band to see its size.

The gel spans the sizes it holds. Its largest band sits at the top and its smallest near the foot, spaced by the logarithm of their size, as a real gel runs them. If a ladder size's label would crowd the one above it, molviz leaves the label off without counting it, but still draws the band.

draw_gel takes no options. molviz draws a gel the same in a file and on a page.

items.title: Leave a lane empty
items.text:
If you expect no band in a lane, such as a water control, give the lane an empty list:

colony_pcr["lanes"].append({"name": "Water", "bands": []})

The gel now has a third lane, and its line in the legend reads "no band":

items.title: Check a gel before you draw it
items.text:
draw_gel checks the gel first. To check it without drawing it, call check_gel. Both raise ValueError, and the message names each problem by its place in the gel. Here a size was typed as text:

colony_pcr["lanes"][0]["bands"] = [160, "838"]
molviz.check_gel(colony_pcr)
# ValueError: lanes[0].bands[1]: must be a number

To write the gel as a PNG or a PDF, see Export SVG, PNG and PDF. To show it in a page with other drawings, see Put drawings in your own page.

items.title: Draw a plate and a stamp
items.text:
A plate drawing shows what each well holds. A stamp drawing shows a transfer: the wells it takes from one plate and the wells it fills on another.

This guide draws plates from AP-1, a project that builds a library of clones on 96-well and 384-well plates.
path: Draw a plate and a stamp

items.title: Name what each well holds
items.text:
Write the plate as a Python dict: its rows, its columns, and wells, which maps each well's name to its contents. A well left out is empty. Rows are lettered from A, and past Z they take two letters, starting with AA and AB. The plate format lists every key.

AP-1's plate picked 1 is a 384-well plate filled in quarters. Each quarter takes every second row and every second column. Quarter 1 holds the odd columns of rows A, C, E to O. Quarter 2 holds the even columns of those rows. Quarter 3 holds the odd columns of rows B, D, F to P. Quarter 4 is empty.

import molviz

wells = {}
for i, row in enumerate("ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOP"):
    for column in range(1, 25):
        quarter = 1 + (column - 1) % 2 + 2 * (i % 2)
        if quarter < 4:
            wells[f"{row}{column}"] = f"quarter {quarter}"

picked = {"title": "picked 1", "rows": 16, "columns": 24, "wells": wells}
molviz.draw_plate(picked).write("picked-1.svg")

The file holds this plate:

Each different contents takes a colour of its own, and the legend under the plate names it. Empty wells are pale grey. Rest the pointer on a well to see its name and contents.

draw_plate takes no options. molviz draws a plate the same in a file and on a page.
path: Draw a plate and a stamp

items.title: Draw a plate with many contents
items.text:
molviz gives a colour of its own to each of up to ten different contents on a plate. Past ten, every filled well takes one colour, and the legend counts the contents in place of naming them. The plate format's colours and legend give the order the colours go in.

AP-1's plate index 1 holds a different pair of primers in each of its 96 wells:

pairs = {
    f"{row}{column}": f"forward {12 * i + column}, reverse 1"
    for i, row in enumerate("ABCDEFGH")
    for column in range(1, 13)
}
index = {"title": "index 1", "rows": 8, "columns": 12, "wells": pairs}
molviz.draw_plate(index).write("index-1.svg")

Rest the pointer on a well to see its contents.
path: Draw a plate and a stamp

items.title: Draw a stamp as two plates
items.text:
A stamp moves one pattern of wells from one plate into another. molviz has no stamp input of its own, so draw a stamp as two plates: the plate it takes from and the plate it fills. Give each well the stamp touches the stamp's title as its contents. Each plate then shows the stamp's wells in one colour, and its legend names the stamp.

AP-1 takes quarter 1 of picked 1 into index 1:

stamp = "Sample a quarter of picked 1 into index 1"
taken = [well for well, contents in wells.items() if contents == "quarter 1"]
filled = [f"{row}{column}" for row in "ABCDEFGH" for column in range(1, 13)]

source = {"title": "From picked 1", "rows": 16, "columns": 24, "wells": dict.fromkeys(taken, stamp)}
target = {"title": "Into index 1", "rows": 8, "columns": 12, "wells": dict.fromkeys(filled, stamp)}
molviz.draw_plate(source).write("from-picked-1.svg")
molviz.draw_plate(target).write("into-index-1.svg")

Start each plate's title with "From" or "Into", so that a reader can tell the two apart.
path: Draw a plate and a stamp

items.title: Check a plate before you draw it
items.text:
draw_plate checks the plate first. To check it without drawing it, call check_plate. Both raise ValueError, and the message names each problem by its place in the plate. Here a well lies past the plate's last row:

molviz.check_plate({"rows": 8, "columns": 12, "wells": {"I1": "water"}})
# ValueError: wells.I1: not on the plate, which runs A1 to H12

To write a plate as a PNG or a PDF, see Export SVG, PNG and PDF. To show plates in a page with other drawings, see Put drawings in your own page.
path: Draw a plate and a stamp

items.title: Export SVG, PNG and PDF
items.text: Write a drawing to a file to put it in slides, a paper or a report. Each draw call returns a drawing, and the drawing's write picks the file's format from its ending. Python writes the file on its own, with no browser and no network.

items.title: Draw what you want to export
items.text:
These examples draw pUC19-GFP, the pUC19 vector with GFP put in by Golden Gate assembly. Save its record, puc19-gfp-product.json, beside your script, or use a record of your own.

import json
from pathlib import Path

import molviz

record = json.loads(Path("puc19-gfp-product.json").read_text())
drawing = molviz.draw(record)

A gel, a plate or a figure works the same way: draw_gel, draw_plate and draw_figure each return a drawing too.

items.title: Write the file
items.text:
Name the file with the ending of the format you want:

drawing.write("puc19-gfp.svg")
drawing.write("puc19-gfp.png")
drawing.write("puc19-gfp.pdf")

Each file holds this drawing:

Pick the format by where the drawing goes:

  • SVG for a web page, or to change the drawing in a vector editor such as Inkscape. Each letter is an outline, so it looks the same on a computer that lacks molviz's fonts.
  • PNG for slides and documents that take an image.
  • PDF for print and for a paper.

The ending is read in any case, so .PDF works too. Any other ending raises ValueError.

A file has no bar of switches. It shows the record with the options you passed to draw. If those options turn on the sequence view, the PDF has the map on its first page and the rows of bases on the pages after it. Write the rows to a PDF gives the steps.

items.title: Set the PNG's resolution
items.text:
write draws a PNG at 300 dots per inch (dpi). To change that, pass dpi:

drawing.write("puc19-gfp.png", dpi=600)

A drawing is measured in points, 72 to the inch, so a PNG prints at the drawing's own size at any dpi. A higher dpi gives more pixels. If the PNG would be too large, write raises ValueError. Write a PDF instead, which stays sharp at any size.

items.title: Write a page instead
items.text:
To write a page that opens in a browser, end the file's name in .html:

drawing.write("puc19-gfp.html")

The page opens offline. A record's page draws it with the viewer, so that the reader can turn the map and switch views. A gel's, a plate's or a figure's page holds its still drawing. To put several drawings in one page, see Put drawings in your own page. Pages, files and still drawings compares a page with each file.

items.title: Show the bases
items.text:
The sequence view sets a record's bases in rows, the top strand over the bottom strand. It draws each feature, primer, cut site and insertion at its own bases, and a CDS with a translation shows its amino acids over its codons. The sequence view hides nothing. This guide turns the view on, narrows it to the bases you need, sets its rows, and writes the rows to a PDF.

The examples draw pUC19-GFP, the pUC19 vector with GFP put in by Golden Gate assembly. Save its record, puc19-gfp-product.json, beside your script, and load it once:

import json
from pathlib import Path

import molviz

record = json.loads(Path("puc19-gfp-product.json").read_text())

Each step shows its code, then the drawing it makes, drawn here from the same record and options. The options table lists every option with its default.

items.title: Turn on the sequence view
items.text:
To draw the sequence view with the map, set sequence_view to True:

molviz.draw(record, sequence_view=True).write("bases.html")

On a page, the reader can also turn the view on and off with the Sequence switch. The view draws at most 100,000 bases, the value of molviz.SEQUENCE_VIEW_LIMIT. For a longer record, give a span, or draw raises ValueError.

items.title: Narrow the view to a span
items.text:
A whole plasmid fills many rows. To show fewer, give a span too. This span holds the M13 site, the ATGA junction and the start of GFP, with GFP's first amino acids over its codons:

molviz.draw(record, span={"start": 340, "end": 520}, sequence_view=True).write("gfp-start.html")

The map draws the same span as a line. On a circular record, a span may run across the origin, as Choose what a map shows explains.

items.title: Set the row length
items.text:
Unless you set bases_per_row, a row on a page holds as many bases as fit its width, from 20 to 100 in steps of 10. A file, a still drawing or a figure holds 60 bases to a row.

To change the row length, set bases_per_row. These rows hold 20 bases each:

junction = {"start": 380, "end": 440}
drawing = molviz.draw(record, span=junction, sequence_view=True, bases_per_row=20)
drawing.write("rows-of-20.html")

When the span doesn't divide into whole rows, the last row holds fewer bases.

items.title: Leave out the bottom strand
items.text:
To draw the top strand alone, set bottom_strand to False:

drawing = molviz.draw(record, span=junction, sequence_view=True, bottom_strand=False)
drawing.write("top-strand.html")

On a page, the reader ticks Both strands to bring the bottom strand back. The rows keep its room, so nothing moves.

items.title: Write the rows to a PDF
items.text:
To print the bases, write the drawing as a PDF:

molviz.draw(record, sequence_view=True).write("pUC19-GFP.pdf")

The PDF holds the drawing from the first step, and it opens in its own viewer, so this page doesn't draw it. The map is on the first page, and the rows are on the pages after it. Each of those pages is as wide as the rows, and holds as many whole rows as fit a page the shape of A4. An SVG or a PNG holds the map and the rows as one tall drawing. Export SVG, PNG and PDF gives the other formats.

items.title: Stack records into a figure
items.text:
A figure is a still drawing to set beside a step of a protocol. It draws one record, or several stacked top to bottom, all with the same options. This guide draws the Golden Gate step that makes pUC19-GFP: its two PCR products over the plasmid they make.

Save their records, gfp-amplicon.json, puc19-backbone-amplicon.json and puc19-gfp-product.json, beside your script, and load them once:

import json
from pathlib import Path

import molviz


def load(name):
    return json.loads(Path(f"{name}.json").read_text())


gfp = load("gfp-amplicon")
backbone = load("puc19-backbone-amplicon")
product = load("puc19-gfp-product")

Each step shows its code, then the figure it makes, drawn here from the same records and options. A figure takes the options that draw takes, which the options table lists. The figure format says what a figure holds.

items.title: Draw one record
items.text:
draw_figure takes a list of records. Given one, it draws that record alone. A circular record drawn whole is a circle:

molviz.draw_figure([product], highlight=["ATGA junction", "TGGC junction"]).write("product.svg")

items.title: Stack several records
items.text:
To stack records, list them in the order to draw them, top first. draw_figure draws each record as draw draws it alone, and sets its name above it. The options apply to every record, and a name in highlight must match something in at least one of them:

molviz.draw_figure(
    [gfp, backbone, product],
    enzymes=["BbsI"],
    highlight=["ATGA overhang", "TGGC overhang", "ATGA junction", "TGGC junction"],
).write("golden-gate.svg")

BbsI cuts each PCR product near both ends, and its cuts leave the overhangs lit on the two lines. The overhangs join to make the junctions lit on the circle. The plasmid holds no BbsI site, so no cut is drawn on it.

items.title: Draw the same stretch of each record
items.text:
To draw one stretch of every record, give a span. Each record keeps its own numbers, and the lines share one scale, so a base number sits at the same place in each line. Records that share their numbering line up, such as a vector before and after a part goes in. AP-1 is a project that builds a library of clones in rounds. Its vector, ap1-block-vector-1.json, takes its first part, N_JUN, in place of a short stuffer to make ap1-round-1.json:

vector = load("ap1-block-vector-1")
round_1 = load("ap1-round-1")
molviz.draw_figure(
    [vector, round_1],
    span={"start": 280, "end": 1262},
    enzymes=["BbsI", "BsaI"],
    highlight=["N_JUN"],
).write("round-1.svg")

Only the lower record holds N_JUN, so the upper one turns pale all over. Each record's line and numbers stay dark.

items.title: Add the bases
items.text:
To draw the bases under each map, set sequence_view to True. Give a short span, so the rows stay few:

molviz.draw_figure(
    [product],
    span={"start": 380, "end": 420},
    sequence_view=True,
    highlight=["ATGA junction"],
).write("atga-junction.pdf")

A figure's PDF puts the maps on its first page. Each record's rows follow on pages of their own, the first of them under the record's name.

items.title: Write the figure
items.text: A figure writes the same files as a single record: .svg, .png and .pdf. Its .html page holds the still drawing and no viewer, so a reader can't zoom it or flip a switch. To put a figure in a page of your own, use still_svg(), which returns the drawing as SVG text. Put drawings in your own page shows how.

items.title: Choose what a map shows
items.text:
A map draws its record's features and primers, the cut sites of each enzyme that cuts it once, and its insertions, reads and disagreements. A track's curves show only in the sequence view. This guide leaves out what your reader doesn't need, picks the enzymes, draws a stretch of the record, and lights the names that matter. Each option sets what the drawing starts with. On a page, the reader can still change it with the switches above the map.

The examples draw pUC19-GFP, the pUC19 vector with GFP put in by Golden Gate assembly. Save its record, puc19-gfp-product.json, beside your script, and load it once:

import json
from pathlib import Path

import molviz

record = json.loads(Path("puc19-gfp-product.json").read_text())

Each step shows its code, then the drawing it makes, drawn here from the same record and options. The options table lists every option with its default.

items.title: Leave out a kind
items.text:
To leave out everything of one kind, name the kind in kinds_off. The kinds are features, primers, cuts, insertions, reads, disagreements and tracks. This map leaves out the primers:

molviz.draw(record, kinds_off=["primers"]).write("no-primers.html")

items.title: Leave out feature types
items.text:
To leave out features by their type, name the types in types_off. This map leaves out the M13 sites, which are primer_bind features, and the MCS and the two junctions, which are misc_feature:

molviz.draw(record, types_off=["primer_bind", "misc_feature"]).write("fewer-features.html")

types_off starts as ["source"], and your list replaces it. If the record has a source feature that you want left out, name source in your list too.

items.title: Name the enzymes to draw
items.text:
A map draws the cut sites of each enzyme that cuts the record once. To draw other enzymes, name them in enzymes. BsaI cuts pUC19-GFP twice, so its sites are left out until you name it:

molviz.draw(record, enzymes=["BsaI"]).write("bsai.html")

Your list replaces the default, so this map draws BsaI's sites and no others. A name matches in any case. molviz draws only the cuts that your record lists, so an enzyme with no cut in the record draws nothing.

items.title: Draw the record as a line
items.text:
A circular record drawn whole opens on the circle. To draw it as a line, set map to "line":

molviz.draw(record, map="line").write("line.html")

items.title: Draw a stretch of the record
items.text:
To draw only some of the bases, give a span with a start and an end. start counts from 0, and the base at end is not drawn. A span is drawn as a line, numbered as the record is. This span holds GFP and the bases on either side of it:

molviz.draw(record, span={"start": 300, "end": 1250}).write("gfp-span.html")

On a circular record, end may pass the record's length to run across the origin. pUC19-GFP has 3,347 bases, so this span holds its last 247 bases and then its first 153:

molviz.draw(record, span={"start": 3100, "end": 3500}).write("origin-span.html")

A span runs at most once around the record. The circle draws a record whole, so map="circle" with a shorter span is an error. Coordinates in the record format gives the rules for counting bases.

items.title: Light the names that matter
items.text:
To light some items and dim the rest, name them in highlight. All else turns one pale grey, and nothing moves. This map lights GFP and the two primers that copy it:

molviz.draw(record, highlight=["GFP", "GFP forward", "GFP reverse"]).write("gfp-lit.html")

A name can be a feature, a primer, an insertion, a read, a disagreement, a track or an enzyme. An enzyme lights every site it cuts. A name matches in any case. If a name matches nothing in the record, draw raises ValueError with the message options.highlight[0]: names nothing in the record.

items.title: Find the hidden labels
items.text:
Where labels would overlap, a drawing hides some of them and counts them in a notice at the bottom right of the map. Labels hide when you ask for more than fits. pUC19-GFP hides nothing, even with every enzyme, so this step draws AP-1's product, ap1-product.json, which holds cuts for 14 enzymes. Drawn on the circle with all of them, some of its cut-site labels hide:

ap1 = json.loads(Path("ap1-product.json").read_text())
every_enzyme = sorted({cut["enzyme"] for cut in ap1["cuts"]})
drawing = molviz.draw(ap1, enzymes=every_enzyme)
print(drawing.notice)
for label in drawing.hidden:
    print(label)

It prints:

6 cut sites are hidden
{'kind': 'cuts', 'name': 'BtgZI', 'at': 1864}
{'kind': 'cuts', 'name': 'BtgZI', 'at': 2233}
{'kind': 'cuts', 'name': 'BtgZI', 'at': 2396}
{'kind': 'cuts', 'name': 'BtgZI', 'at': 2577}
{'kind': 'cuts', 'name': 'BspQI - SapI', 'at': 2295}
{'kind': 'cuts', 'name': 'BspQI - SapI', 'at': 2505}

The drawing's notice is the sentence that the drawing shows, and hidden lists each hidden label in the shape that Hidden labels gives.

On a page, rest the pointer on the notice to list the hidden labels. The page lays the labels out again each time the reader turns the circle or flips a switch, so the count can change:

To bring a hidden label back, draw less: leave out a kind, name fewer enzymes, or draw a span. A lit label is the last to hide, so highlight keeps the labels that matter in view. How a drawing stays readable gives the order in which labels hide.

items.title: Put drawings in your own page
items.text:
Put molviz's drawings in a page you build, such as a report that holds a map, a gel and a plate. The page needs no build step and no network. Show each drawing in one of two ways:

  • Live, with the viewer. The reader can turn and zoom a map, switch its views and read its bases. The page carries the viewer's script.
  • Still, as SVG written into the page. It looks the same as a live drawing, and its hovers show, but the reader can't change it. The page needs no script.

For one drawing on a page of its own, drawing.write("name.html") is enough. See Export SVG, PNG and PDF.
path: Put drawings in your own page

items.title: Draw live with the viewer
items.text:
1. Put viewer_script() in a <script> element, once.
  2. After it, call molviz.draw(element, record, options) for each record. The drawing is added at the end of the element.

This Python writes a page that draws pUC19-GFP live. Save its record, puc19-gfp-product.json, beside your script.

import json
from pathlib import Path

import molviz

record = json.loads(Path("puc19-gfp-product.json").read_text())
options = {"map": "line", "highlight": ["GFP"]}


def script_json(value):
    """Return value as JSON that a <script> element holds safely."""
    return json.dumps(value).replace("<", "\\u003c")


page = f"""<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
<meta charset="utf-8">
<title>pUC19-GFP</title>
</head>
<body>
<div id="map"></div>
<script>{molviz.viewer_script()}</script>
<script>
molviz.draw(document.getElementById("map"), {script_json(record)}, {script_json(options)});
</script>
</body>
</html>
"""
Path("puc19-gfp-page.html").write_text(page)

script_json writes each < as an escape, so that a name holding </script> can't end the script early. The page draws this:

Each record has a bar of switches above its map. A print of the page leaves the bar out.

The other inputs have draw calls of their own: molviz.drawGel(element, gel), molviz.drawPlate(element, plate) and molviz.drawFigure(element, records, options).
path: Put drawings in your own page

items.title: Write still drawings with the font rules
items.text:
1. Put font_rules() in a <style> element, once.
  2. Write each drawing's still_svg() into the page as it is.

This writes a page that holds a gel and a plate: the colony PCR from Draw a gel and plate picked 1 from Draw a plate and a stamp. Save their files, golden-gate-colony-pcr.json and ap1-picked-1.json, beside your script.

import json
from pathlib import Path

import molviz

colony_pcr = json.loads(Path("golden-gate-colony-pcr.json").read_text())
picked = json.loads(Path("ap1-picked-1.json").read_text())
drawings = [molviz.draw_gel(colony_pcr), molviz.draw_plate(picked)]
stills = "\n".join(drawing.still_svg() for drawing in drawings)
page = f"""<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
<meta charset="utf-8">
<title>Colony PCR</title>
<style>{molviz.font_rules()}</style>
</head>
<body>
{stills}
</body>
</html>
"""
Path("colony-pcr-page.html").write_text(page)

The page shows these:

The font rules load molviz's fonts from the page itself. Without them, the browser draws the text in a font of its own, which may not fit the space laid out for it.

If the page also draws live, leave the font rules out. Each draw call adds them, and a second copy only makes the page larger.
path: Put drawings in your own page

items.title: Make a still drawing in the browser
items.text:
A page that carries the viewer can make still drawings itself. Each input has a still call: molviz.stillSvg(record, options), molviz.gelStillSvg(gel), molviz.plateStillSvg(plate) and molviz.figureStillSvg(records, options). Each returns an object whose svg is the SVG text. Call molviz.declareFaces(document) once, to add the font rules to the page.

In this code, the variable gel holds the colony PCR gel, parsed from golden-gate-colony-pcr.json. The code draws it into the element whose id is gel:

const { svg } = molviz.gelStillSvg(gel);
molviz.declareFaces(document);
document.getElementById("gel").insertAdjacentHTML("beforeend", svg);

The element then holds this still drawing:

Don't call molviz.svg, molviz.gelSvg, molviz.plateSvg or molviz.figureSvg in a page. They write the SVG for a file, which needs letter outlines that a page doesn't load, so they throw an error.

The JavaScript API lists every name on the molviz object.
path: Put drawings in your own page

items.title: Figure format
items.text:
A figure is one record, or several stacked top to bottom, all drawn with one set of options. In Python a figure is a list of records, which molviz.draw_figure draws. In a page it is a JSON array of records, which the global molviz.checkFigure checks and molviz.drawFigure draws. Both run the same check.

The check reports every problem it finds, each named by its path from records, such as records[1].bases: must hold at least one base. Python raises ValueError, and the page's check throws a FormatError.

Stack records into a figure draws figures in this format.

items.title: Example
items.text:
This figure stacks two linear records, each with one feature, and lights the feature named insert.

[
  {
    "name": "vector",
    "circular": false,
    "bases": "GAATTCAAAAAAAAAAGGATCC",
    "features": [
      {"name": "stuffer", "type": "misc_feature", "strand": 0, "segments": [{"start": 6, "end": 16}]}
    ]
  },
  {
    "name": "vector with insert",
    "circular": false,
    "bases": "GAATTCATGAGCAAAGGCGAAGAACTGTAAGGATCC",
    "features": [
      {"name": "insert", "type": "CDS", "strand": 1, "segments": [{"start": 6, "end": 30}]}
    ]
  }
]

Its options are {"highlight": ["insert"]}.

items.title: The figure
items.text:
Part Type Required Default Meaning the list list of records, at least one yes Each item is a record in the record format. The first is drawn at the top.

When two or more records stack, each record's name is written over it. A page written from the figure takes the records' names, joined by commas, as its title.

items.title: Options
items.text:
A figure takes the options a record takes, once, and draws every record with them.

  • molviz checks each option against each record. A span must fit every record, and "map": "circle" needs every record to be circular and drawn whole.
  • A name in highlight must name something in at least one record.
  • An option left out takes its default for each record on its own. Each circular record drawn whole is a circle, and each record shows the enzymes that cut it once.
  • A problem that only some records have names them after its path, such as options.span.end (records[0]).

items.title: Gel format
items.text:
A gel is a simulated agarose gel: a ladder and sample lanes, each band at its size in base pairs. It holds no record. In Python a gel is a dict, which molviz.check_gel checks and molviz.draw_gel draws. In a page it is a JSON object, which the global molviz.checkGel checks and molviz.drawGel draws. Both run the same check.

The check reports every problem it finds, each named by its path, such as ladder.bands[1]: must be 1 or more. Python raises ValueError, and the page's check throws a FormatError. A key that is not on this page is an error. The types are the ones on the record format page.

Draw a gel writes a gel in this format and draws it.

items.title: Example
items.text:
This is the colony PCR gel of pUC19-GFP: a correct clone and an empty vector beside a 100 bp ladder.

{
 "title": "Colony PCR",
 "ladder": {
  "name": "NEB 100 bp DNA Ladder (N3231)",
  "bands": [
   100,
   200,
   300,
   400,
   500,
   600,
   700,
   800,
   900,
   1000,
   1200,
   1517
  ]
 },
 "lanes": [
  {
   "name": "Correct clone",
   "bands": [
    160,
    838
   ]
  },
  {
   "name": "Empty vector",
   "bands": [
    177
   ]
  }
 ]
}

items.title: The gel
items.text: Key Type Required Default Meaning title text no none The title drawn over the gel. A page written from the gel takes it as the page's title, or "Gel" when there is none. ladder ladder yes The size marker in the first lane. lanes list of lanes yes The sample lanes, left to right after the ladder. The list may be empty.

items.title: Ladder
items.text:
ladder is an object with these keys.

Key Type Required Default Meaning name text yes The ladder's name, such as NEB 100 bp DNA Ladder (N3231). bands list of integers, each 1 or more, at least one yes The ladder's band sizes in base pairs.

The drawing marks the ladder's lane L and writes the ladder's sizes beside the gel. It leaves out the label of a size that would crowd the one above it, and does not count it. It still draws that size's band.

items.title: Lanes
items.text:
Each item of lanes is an object with these keys.

Key Type Required Default Meaning name text yes The lane's name, written in the legend. bands list of integers, each 1 or more yes The lane's band sizes in base pairs. An empty list is a lane with no band.

The drawing numbers the lanes from 1 in the order given. Each lane has a line in the legend under the gel, with its name and its sizes in the order given, or "no band".

items.title: Where a band runs
items.text: A band's height follows the logarithm of its size. The largest band on the gel, in any lane, runs the least far and the smallest runs the farthest. When every band on the gel has one size, each runs halfway.

items.title: JavaScript API
items.text: The viewer is one script. Running it defines one global, molviz, and this page lists every name on it. Python's viewer_script() returns the script's text, for a page to put in a <script> element. Put drawings in your own page uses these calls.

items.title: Each input's four calls
items.text:
Each input has four calls. One checks it, one draws it into an element of a page, one returns it as SVG for a file, and one returns it as a still SVG.

Input Check Draw into an element File SVG Still SVG A record check draw svg stillSvg A figure checkFigure drawFigure figureSvg figureStillSvg A gel checkGel drawGel gelSvg gelStillSvg A plate checkPlate drawPlate plateSvg plateStillSvg

Each call takes the input as a plain object, in the format Python's calls take, which each input's format page gives. A figure's input is a list of one or more records.

A record's calls and a figure's calls take options as one object, such as {"map": "line"}. They are the options that Python's draw takes by name. A figure's options apply to every record in it. A gel's calls and a plate's calls accept options and ignore them. Left out, options is {}, so each option takes its default.

items.title: Check
items.text:
molviz.check(record)

check, checkFigure, checkGel and checkPlate return a checked copy of the input and leave the input as it was. A record comes back with each list it left out set to [], and so does each record of a figure.

Each throws a FormatError when the input breaks its format.

items.title: Draw into an element
items.text:
molviz.draw(element, record, options)

draw, drawFigure, drawGel and drawPlate add the drawing at the end of element, a DOM element, after what it already holds. Letters are real text. Each call first adds the font rules to the page with declareFaces.

  • draw opens the record in a frame: a bar of switches, the map, and the sequence view when sequence_view is true.
  • drawFigure, drawGel and drawPlate each add one SVG element, with no switches.

Where a span holds more than SEQUENCE_VIEW_LIMIT bases, draw and drawFigure leave the sequence view out instead of throwing.

Each returns an object with one method, destroy(). It removes the drawing and leaves the font rules for any other drawing on the page. A second call does nothing.

Each throws a FormatError that names every problem in the input. When the input is right, the error names every problem in the options instead.

items.title: File SVG
items.text:
molviz.svg(record, options)

svg, figureSvg, gelSvg and plateSvg are for code that writes files. Each letter is an outline, so the SVG looks the same on a machine without molviz's fonts.

These four calls need the outline script, which ships beside the viewer, to have run first. Without it, they throw an Error whose message is molviz: a file's outlines need the outline script. A page uses the draw calls and the still calls, which need only the viewer.

Each returns an object with four keys:

Key Type What it holds svg string The whole drawing as SVG text. Its width and height have no unit. One unit is one point. pages array of strings One SVG for each PDF page. With the sequence view, the map is the first page and the rows follow. Otherwise it holds one SVG, the same as svg. hidden array of objects The labels left out because they would overlap, as Hidden labels describes. notice string The hidden-label notice as a sentence, such as 3 cut sites and 1 primer are hidden. It is empty when nothing hides.

A gel's hidden and a plate's hidden are [], and their notice is "", even when a gel leaves out the label of a crowded ladder size.

Each throws a FormatError as the draw calls do. It also throws one when sequence_view is true for a span of more than SEQUENCE_VIEW_LIMIT bases.

items.title: Still SVG
items.text:
molviz.stillSvg(record, options)
